solution:
Each rate of change is divided by the stoichiometric coefficient of that species, and a minus sign is attached to a reactant because its concentration falls with time. For \(\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3\,H_2(g) \longrightarrow 2\,NH_3(g)}\) the coefficients are \(1\), \(3\) and \(2\), so

rate of reaction \(= -\dfrac{d[\mathrm{N_2}]}{dt} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{H_2}]}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{NH_3}]}{dt}\)

In words, hydrogen is consumed three times as fast as nitrogen and ammonia is formed twice as fast as nitrogen is consumed.

[Textbook misprint: the organic product is printed as \(\mathrm{CH_3OH^{\ominus}}\), carrying a negative charge. Methanol is a neutral molecule, so the product should be \(\mathrm{CH_3OH}\); as printed the equation also does not balance in charge. The rate law and the answer are unaffected.]

The rate law rate \(= k[\mathrm{CH_3Br}][\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}]\) is first order in each reactant, so the rate is directly proportional to each concentration.

a. If \([\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}]\) is decreased by a factor of \(5\) while \([\mathrm{CH_3Br}]\) is unchanged, the rate is also decreased by a factor of \(5\), that is it falls to one fifth of its original value.

b. If both concentrations are doubled the rate changes by a factor \(2 \times 2 = 4\), so the rate increases to four times its original value.

In general there is no relationship between them. Section 6.3.1 states that the powers \(x\) and \(y\) of the concentration terms in the rate law are not necessarily equal to the stoichiometric coefficients \(a\) and \(b\) of the balanced equation; they are determined experimentally and cannot be predicted from the stoichiometry of an overall reaction.

The coefficients are the exponents only when the reaction is an **elementary** reaction, that is one that occurs in a single step. Section 6.4.3 gives the example \(\mathrm{2NO_2(g) \longrightarrow 2NO(g) + O_2(g)}\), whose experimentally found rate law is rate \(= k[\mathrm{NO_2}]^2\), the exponent matching the coefficient \(2\). The same applies to the rate determining step of a complex reaction, whose rate law may be written from its own stoichiometry.

A collision leads to reaction only if two conditions are met at once. First, the colliding molecules must possess kinetic energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, since the reactants have to climb the energy barrier before they can be converted to products (sections 6.6.2 and 6.6.4). Second, they must be properly oriented relative to each other so that the reacting groups approach closely (section 6.6.3).

Collisions that fail either condition are unsuccessful: the molecules simply collide and separate again. That is why only a small fraction of the very large number of collisions actually produces product.

The activation energy is the minimum kinetic energy that the colliding reactant molecules must possess in order for the reaction to occur (section 6.6.2). Equivalently, as section 6.6.4 puts it, it is the height of the energy barrier between the reactants and the products, which the reactant molecules must climb before they are converted into products. It is denoted \(E_a\).

The units follow from \(k = \dfrac{\text{rate}}{[\mathrm{A}]^n}\), where the rate has units \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\) and each concentration \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\).

For a zero order reaction \(n = 0\), so \(k\) has the same units as the rate itself:

\(k = \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\)

For a second order reaction \(n = 2\):

\(k = \dfrac{\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}}{(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}})^{2}} = \mathrm{mol^{-1}\ L\ s^{-1}}\)

A complex reaction takes place as a series of elementary steps, and one of these steps is slower than the others. That slowest step is the rate determining step (section 6.4.4). Because the overall reaction can proceed no faster than its slowest stage, this step determines the rate of the overall reaction, and the rate law of the overall reaction is the rate law of this step.

For a first order reaction, Eq. (6.10) gives

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}\)  or  \(k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}\)

For a zero order reaction, Eq. (6.16) gives

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2k}\)  or  \(k = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2\,t_{1/2}}\)

where \([\mathrm{A}]_0\) is the initial concentration of the reactant.

For a first order reaction \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}\). The initial concentration does not appear in this expression, so the half life is **independent** of the initial concentration of the reactant and stays the same however much reactant is taken.

For a zero order reaction \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2k}\). Here the half life is **directly proportional** to the initial concentration, so doubling the initial concentration doubles the half life.

The concentration of a reactant or of a product is measured at a series of times and plotted against time, as in Fig. 6.1. A tangent is then drawn to the resulting curve at the particular time instant \(t_1\) of interest. The slope of that tangent gives the rate of the reaction at that instant.

In symbols, the instantaneous rate is obtained by replacing the average rate \(\Delta c/\Delta t\) by the derivative \(dc/dt\), so that for \(\mathrm{A \longrightarrow B}\)

instantaneous rate \(= -\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = \dfrac{d[\mathrm{B}]}{dt}\)

The chapter notes that in chemical kinetics we are concerned with instantaneous rates rather than average rates.

| Order | Molecularity |
|---|---|
| It is an experimentally determined property. | It is a theoretical entity. |
| It is the sum of powers of the concentration terms of reactants those appear in the rate equation. | It is the number of reactant molecules taking part in an elementary reaction. |
| It may be an integer, fraction or zero. | It is an integer. |

The chapter adds that for an elementary reaction the order and the molecularity may be the same, as in \(\mathrm{2NO_2 \longrightarrow 2NO + O_2}\), which is bimolecular and second order, but that in general they need not be.

a. Adding the two steps and cancelling the species that appears on both sides gives the overall reaction

\(\mathrm{2\,NO(g) + Cl_2(g) \longrightarrow 2\,NOCl(g)}\)

b. \(\mathrm{NOCl_2}\) is produced in step 1 and consumed in step 2, and it does not appear in the overall equation. It is therefore the reaction intermediate.

c. Step 1 has two reactant molecules, one \(\mathrm{NO}\) and one \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\), so its molecularity is two, that is it is bimolecular. Step 2 also has two reactant molecules, one \(\mathrm{NOCl_2}\) and one \(\mathrm{NO}\), so it too is bimolecular.

The integrated rate law for a first order reaction is

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\)

The half life \(t_{1/2}\) is the time required for the reactant concentration to fall to one half of its initial value, so at \(t = t_{1/2}\) we have \([\mathrm{A}]_t = [\mathrm{A}]_0/2\). Putting this condition into the integrated rate law,

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t_{1/2}}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_0/2} = \dfrac{2.303}{t_{1/2}}\log_{10} 2 = \dfrac{2.303}{t_{1/2}} \times 0.3010\)

Hence

\(k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}\)  and  \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}\)   …… Eq. (6.10)

The initial concentration has cancelled out, which is why the half life of a first order reaction is independent of the initial concentration of the reactant.

The integrated rate law of a zero order reaction, Eq. (6.15), rearranges to Eq. (6.17):

\([\mathrm{A}]_t = -k\,t + [\mathrm{A}]_0\)

Comparing with \(y = mx + c\), the quantity \([\mathrm{A}]_t\) is \(y\), the time \(t\) is \(x\), the slope \(m\) is \(-k\) and the intercept \(c\) is \([\mathrm{A}]_0\).

A zero order reaction is therefore represented by plotting \([\mathrm{A}]_t\) along the vertical axis against time along the horizontal axis. The plot is a **straight line with a negative slope**, as in Fig. 6.6. The slope of the line is \(-k\), so the rate constant is obtained as the negative of the slope, and the intercept on the vertical axis gives the initial concentration \([\mathrm{A}]_0\).

Pseudo-first order reactions are reactions which are expected to be of a higher order but which are found to follow first order kinetics (section 6.5.9).

**Example** — the hydrolysis of methyl acetate:

\(\mathrm{CH_3COOCH_3(aq) + H_2O(\mathit{l}) \longrightarrow CH_3COOH(aq) + CH_3OH(aq)}\)

The rate law is rate \(= k'[\mathrm{CH_3COOCH_3}][\mathrm{H_2O}]\), so the reaction is expected to be of second order.

**Why it is pseudo-first order** — water is the solvent and is present in such large excess that the change in its concentration during the reaction is negligible compared with its initial value, so \([\mathrm{H_2O}]\) remains effectively constant. Writing \([\mathrm{H_2O}] = k''\), the rate law becomes

rate \(= k'\,[\mathrm{CH_3COOCH_3}]\,k'' = k\,[\mathrm{CH_3COOCH_3}]\)  where \(k = k'k''\)

The rate now depends on only one concentration term, so the reaction is of first order.

Two requirements must be satisfied together.

i. **Sufficient energy.** The colliding reactant molecules must possess a minimum kinetic energy, the activation energy \(E_a\). Only molecules whose kinetic energy is equal to or greater than \(E_a\) can overcome the energy barrier between reactants and products; the fraction of such molecules is \(f = e^{-E_a/RT}\).

ii. **Proper orientation.** The molecules must be so oriented relative to each other that the reacting groups approach closely. The chapter illustrates this with \(\mathrm{A + C\text{-}B \longrightarrow A\text{-}B + C}\): if A approaches the C end no reaction occurs and the molecules merely collide and separate, whereas if A approaches the B end the collision is successful.

A collision that meets both requirements is a successful collision. Because relatively few collisions meet both, only a small fraction of all collisions leads to products.

A catalyst is a substance added to the reactants that increases the rate of reaction without itself being consumed. It works by providing an **alternative pathway associated with a lower activation energy**, not by supplying energy to the molecules.

The potential energy diagram of Fig. 6.10 makes this clear. Two energy profiles are drawn between the same reactants and the same products, and the reaction coordinate is plotted along the horizontal axis with energy along the vertical axis. The barrier for the uncatalysed reaction, \((E_a)_1\), is the taller of the two; the barrier for the same reaction in the presence of the catalyst, \((E_a)_2\), is lower. Both curves begin and end at the same energies, so the catalyst lowers the barrier without altering the reactants or the products.

Because the fraction of molecules with energy at least \(E_a\) is \(f = e^{-E_a/RT}\), lowering \(E_a\) raises that fraction sharply. Many more molecules can therefore cross the barrier and the rate of the catalysed reaction is larger than that of the uncatalysed one.

The chapter's own illustration is the decomposition of \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\) in aqueous solution: the activation energy is \(76\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) without a catalyst and falls to \(57\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) in the presence of iodide ion, and the reaction is correspondingly faster.

The Arrhenius equation, Eq. (6.18), is \(k = \mathrm{A}\,e^{-E_a/RT}\), and taking logarithms gives Eq. (6.19),

\(\ln k = -\dfrac{E_a}{RT} + \ln \mathrm{A}\)

Since the rate is proportional to \(k\), whatever raises \(k\) raises the rate.

**(a) Effect of temperature.** \(T\) appears in the denominator of the exponent. As \(T\) increases, \(E_a/RT\) decreases, so \(-E_a/RT\) becomes less negative and the exponential factor \(e^{-E_a/RT}\) increases. Hence \(k\) increases and the rate of reaction increases with a rise in temperature. Physically, a higher temperature means a larger fraction of molecules possessing energy at least \(E_a\).

**(b) Effect of activation energy.** \(E_a\) appears with a negative sign in the exponent. At a fixed temperature, a larger \(E_a\) makes \(-E_a/RT\) more negative, so \(e^{-E_a/RT}\) and therefore \(k\) become smaller and the reaction is slower. Conversely a smaller \(E_a\), such as that provided by a catalyst, gives a larger \(k\) and a faster reaction.

Consider the first order reaction

\(\mathrm{A \longrightarrow product}\)   …… (6.3)

The differential rate law is

rate \(= -\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = k\,[\mathrm{A}]\)   …… (6.4)

where \([\mathrm{A}]\) is the concentration of reactant at time \(t\). Rearranging Eq. (6.4),

\(\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{[\mathrm{A}]} = -k\,dt\)   …… (6.5)

Let \([\mathrm{A}]_0\) be the initial concentration of A at \(t = 0\) and \([\mathrm{A}]_t\) its concentration at time \(t\). Integrating Eq. (6.5) between these limits,

\(\displaystyle\int_{[\mathrm{A}]_0}^{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{[\mathrm{A}]} = -k\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t} dt\)

On integration, \(\Big[\ln[\mathrm{A}]\Big]_{[\mathrm{A}]_0}^{[\mathrm{A}]_t} = -k\,(t)_0^{t}\)

Substitution of limits gives

\(\ln[\mathrm{A}]_t - \ln[\mathrm{A}]_0 = -k\,t\)

or \(\ln\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_t}{[\mathrm{A}]_0} = -kt\)   …… (6.6)

or \(k = \dfrac{1}{t}\ln\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\)

Converting the natural logarithm to base \(10\),

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\)   …… (6.7)

which is the integrated rate law for a first order reaction. Taking the antilogarithm of Eq. (6.6) gives the equivalent exponential form

\(\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_t}{[\mathrm{A}]_0} = e^{-kt}\)  or  \([\mathrm{A}]_t = [\mathrm{A}]_0 e^{-kt}\)   …… (6.8)

and if \(a\) is the initial concentration and \(x\) the concentration that has reacted in time \(t\), so that \([\mathrm{A}]_t = (a - x)\),

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{a}{(a-x)}\)   …… (6.9)

A first order reaction can be represented graphically in three ways, each of which yields a straight line.

i. **Rate against concentration.** The differential rate law is rate \(= -\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = k[\mathrm{A}]_t + 0\), which has the form \(y = mx + c\) with \(c = 0\). A plot of rate against \([\mathrm{A}]_t\) is therefore a straight line passing through the origin whose slope is \(k\) (Fig. 6.3).

ii. **\(\log_{10}[\mathrm{A}]_t\) against time.** Rearranging Eq. (6.7) gives

\(\log_{10}[\mathrm{A}]_t = -\dfrac{k}{2.303}t + \log_{10}[\mathrm{A}]_0\)

A graph of \(\log_{10}[\mathrm{A}]_t\) against \(t\) is a straight line of slope \(-k/2.303\) with intercept \(\log_{10}[\mathrm{A}]_0\) on the vertical axis (Fig. 6.4). The line slopes downwards because the reactant is being used up.

iii. **\(\log_{10}([\mathrm{A}]_0/[\mathrm{A}]_t)\) against time.** Eq. (6.7) also gives

\(\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t} = \dfrac{k}{2.303}t\)

which has the form \(y = mx\). The graph is a straight line passing through the origin with slope \(k/2.303\) (Fig. 6.5).

For the gas phase reaction \(\mathrm{A(g) \longrightarrow B(g) + C(g)}\), let the initial pressure of A be \(P_i\) and let it decrease by \(x\) within time \(t\).

Pressure of the reactant A at time \(t\):

\(P_A = P_i - x\)   …… (6.11)

One mole of A gives one mole of B and one mole of C, so the pressures of the products at time \(t\) are

\(P_B = P_C = x\)

The total pressure at time \(t\) is then

\(P = P_i - x + x + x = P_i + x\)

Hence \(x = P - P_i\)   …… (6.12)

Substituting Eq. (6.12) into Eq. (6.11) gives the pressure of A at time \(t\):

\(P_A = P_i - (P - P_i) = P_i - P + P_i = 2P_i - P\)

The integrated rate law for a first order reaction is

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\)

At constant volume and temperature the concentration of a gas is proportional to its partial pressure, so the concentrations may be expressed in terms of pressures:

\([\mathrm{A}]_0 = P_i\)  and  \([\mathrm{A}]_t = P_A = 2P_i - P\)

Substitution gives

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{P_i}{2P_i - P}\)   …… (6.13)

where \(P\) is the total pressure of the reaction mixture at time \(t\).

**Zeroth order reaction.** A zero order reaction is one whose rate is independent of the concentration of the reactant (section 6.5.8).

**Integrated rate law.** For the zero order reaction \(\mathrm{A \longrightarrow P}\) the differential rate law is

rate \(= -\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = k\,[\mathrm{A}]^0 = k\)   …… (6.14)

Rearrangement gives

\(d[\mathrm{A}] = -k\,dt\)

Integrating between the limits \([\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_0\) at \(t = 0\) and \([\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_t\) at \(t = t\),

\(\displaystyle\int_{[\mathrm{A}]_0}^{[\mathrm{A}]_t} d[\mathrm{A}] = -k\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t} dt\)

or \([\mathrm{A}]_t - [\mathrm{A}]_0 = -kt\)

Hence \(k\,t = [\mathrm{A}]_0 - [\mathrm{A}]_t\)   …… (6.15)

or \(k = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0 - [\mathrm{A}]_t}{t}\)

**Units of the rate constant.**

\(k = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0 - [\mathrm{A}]_t}{t} = \dfrac{\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}}{t} = \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ t^{-1}}\)

so with time in seconds the units are \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ s^{-1}}\). The units of the rate constant of a zero order reaction are thus the same as those of the rate itself.

**(a) Graphically, using the Arrhenius equation.** Taking logarithms of \(k = \mathrm{A}\,e^{-E_a/RT}\) and converting to base \(10\) gives Eq. (6.20):

\(\log_{10}k = -\dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\cdot\dfrac{1}{T} + \log_{10}\mathrm{A}\)

This has the form \(y = mx + c\) with \(y = \log_{10}k\) and \(x = 1/T\). The rate constant is therefore measured at several temperatures and \(\log_{10}k\) is plotted against \(1/T\). The Arrhenius plot so obtained is a straight line (Fig. 6.8) whose slope is

slope \(= -\dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\)

and whose intercept is \(\log_{10}\mathrm{A}\). Measuring the slope gives

\(E_a = -2.303\,R \times \text{slope}\)

**(b) From rate constants at two different temperatures.** If \(k_1\) and \(k_2\) are the rate constants at temperatures \(T_1\) and \(T_2\), Eq. (6.20) written at each temperature gives Eqs. (6.21) and (6.22), and subtracting one from the other gives Eq. (6.23):

\(\log_{10}\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left(\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2}\right)\)

Since \(k_1\), \(k_2\), \(T_1\), \(T_2\) and \(R\) are all known, \(E_a\) is obtained as

\(E_a = \dfrac{2.303\,R\,T_1T_2}{T_2 - T_1}\log_{10}\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}\)

The average kinetic energy of molecules is proportional to temperature, and a bimolecular reaction occurs only when the colliding molecules possess kinetic energy of at least \(E_a\). The effect of temperature is therefore shown by plotting the fraction of molecules having a given kinetic energy along the vertical axis against kinetic energy along the horizontal axis, for two different temperatures \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) with \(T_2 > T_1\). This is Fig. 6.9.

Each curve rises to a maximum and then falls away. The curve for the higher temperature \(T_2\) is flatter and its maximum is shifted towards higher energy, so it is broader on the high energy side.

The area under a curve is proportional to the number of molecules having those values of kinetic energy, and the total area is the same at \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) because the total number of molecules is unchanged. The shaded areas beyond \(E_a\) represent the fractions of molecules whose energy exceeds \(E_a\) at the two temperatures, and the area for \(T_2\) is clearly the larger.

Hence, with an increase of temperature the fraction of molecules having energy equal to or greater than \(E_a\) increases, more collisions are successful, and the rate of the reaction increases.

The effect of a catalyst is shown by Fig. 6.11, a plot of the fraction of molecules \(\left(\dfrac{dn}{N}\right)\) along the vertical axis against energy along the horizontal axis, with the threshold energy marked in two places: \((E_a)_1\) before the use of the catalyst and \((E_a)_2\) in the presence of the catalyst.

A single distribution curve is drawn, since the catalyst does not change the temperature and therefore does not change the energy distribution of the molecules. What the catalyst changes is the position of the threshold: it **lowers** the threshold energy, so \((E_a)_2\) lies to the left of \((E_a)_1\).

The shaded area to the right of a threshold gives the fraction of molecules that can cross the barrier. Because \((E_a)_2\) is the smaller threshold, the area beyond it is the larger, so more molecules acquire the minimum amount of energy needed and tend to cross the energy barrier.

The fraction of activated molecules is thus greater for the catalysed reaction, and the rate of the catalysed reaction is larger than that of the reaction with no catalyst.

(The complementary picture is Fig. 6.10, in which the catalysed reaction is shown to follow an alternative pathway whose potential energy barrier is the lower of the two.)

Let the rate law be rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}]^x[\mathrm{B}]^y\).

**Order with respect to A.** Compare experiments 1 and 2, in which \([\mathrm{B}]\) is held at \(0.05\ \mathrm{M}\). \([\mathrm{A}]\) goes from \(0.3\) to \(0.6\ \mathrm{M}\), a factor of \(2\), and the rate goes from \(0.15\) to \(0.30\ \mathrm{M\ s^{-1}}\), also a factor of \(2\). Hence \(2^x = 2\) and \(x = 1\).

**Order with respect to B.** Compare experiments 2 and 3, in which \([\mathrm{A}]\) is held at \(0.6\ \mathrm{M}\). \([\mathrm{B}]\) goes from \(0.05\) to \(0.2\ \mathrm{M}\), a factor of \(4\), and the rate goes from \(0.30\) to \(1.20\ \mathrm{M\ s^{-1}}\), also a factor of \(4\). Hence \(4^y = 4\) and \(y = 1\).

**Rate law.**

rate \(= k\,[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]\)

The reaction is first order in A, first order in B and second order overall. Note that the order in A is \(1\) although the coefficient of A in the equation is \(2\); the order is an experimental quantity and is not read off the stoichiometry.

**Rate constant.** From experiment 1,

\(k = \dfrac{\text{rate}}{[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]} = \dfrac{0.15\ \mathrm{M\ s^{-1}}}{0.3\ \mathrm{M} \times 0.05\ \mathrm{M}} = 10\ \mathrm{M^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\)

The same value is obtained from the other two rows, which confirms the rate law.

Given : \([\mathrm{A}]_0 = 20\ \mathrm{mmol\ dm^{-3}}\), \([\mathrm{A}]_t = 8\ \mathrm{mmol\ dm^{-3}}\), \(t = 38\) min, \(t_{1/2} = ?\)

For a first order reaction,

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\)

\(= \dfrac{2.303}{38\ \mathrm{min}}\log_{10}\dfrac{20}{8} = \dfrac{2.303}{38}\log_{10} 2.5\)

\(= \dfrac{2.303 \times 0.3979}{38} = 0.02412\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

(The concentrations may be left in \(\mathrm{mmol\ dm^{-3}}\) because only their ratio is used.)

Hence

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.02412\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}} = 28.7\ \mathrm{min}\)

The half life of the reaction is \(28.7\) minutes.

Given : \(t_{1/2} = 1.7\) hours, \(20\%\) of the reactant has reacted, \(t = ?\)

First obtain the rate constant from the half life:

\(k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{1.7\ \mathrm{h}} = 0.4076\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}\)

If \(20\%\) has reacted then \(80\%\) remains, so taking \([\mathrm{A}]_0 = 100\) gives \([\mathrm{A}]_t = 80\).

\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t} = \dfrac{2.303}{0.4076\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}}\log_{10}\dfrac{100}{80}\)

\(= \dfrac{2.303}{0.4076} \times \log_{10} 1.25 = \dfrac{2.303 \times 0.0969}{0.4076} = 0.5475\ \mathrm{h}\)

\(= 0.5475 \times 60 = 32.9\ \mathrm{min}\)

It will take \(32.9\) minutes, that is about \(0.55\) hour.

Given : \(E_a = 104\ \mathrm{kJ/mol} = 104 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J/mol}\), \(k_1 = 3.7 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\) at \(T_1 = 25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C} = 298\ \mathrm{K}\), \(T_2 = 30\ ^\circ\mathrm{C} = 303\ \mathrm{K}\), \(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\), \(k_2 = ?\)

Using Eq. (6.23),

\(\log_{10}\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left(\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2}\right)\)

\(= \dfrac{104 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}}{2.303 \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}mol^{-1}}}\left(\dfrac{303\ \mathrm{K} - 298\ \mathrm{K}}{298\ \mathrm{K} \times 303\ \mathrm{K}}\right)\)

\(= 5432 \times \dfrac{5}{90294} = 5432 \times 5.537 \times 10^{-5} = 0.3008\)

\(\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \text{antilog } 0.3008 = 1.999 \approx 2\)

Hence

\(k_2 = 2 \times 3.7 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} = 7.4 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)

The rate constant at \(30\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) is \(7.4 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\); a rise of only \(5\ \mathrm{K}\) has roughly doubled it.

Given : \(T_1 = 303\ \mathrm{K}\), \(T_2 = 313\ \mathrm{K}\), \(\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = 2\), \(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\), \(E_a = ?\)

From Eq. (6.23),

\(\log_{10}\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left(\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2}\right)\)

Rearranging for \(E_a\),

\(E_a = \dfrac{2.303\,R\,T_1T_2}{T_2 - T_1}\log_{10}\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}\)

\(= \dfrac{2.303 \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}mol^{-1}} \times 303\ \mathrm{K} \times 313\ \mathrm{K}}{313\ \mathrm{K} - 303\ \mathrm{K}} \times \log_{10} 2\)

\(= \dfrac{19.15 \times 94839}{10} \times 0.3010\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(= 54664\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}} = 54.66\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

The energy of activation is \(54.66\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}\).

Given : \(T = 500\ ^\circ\mathrm{C} = 500 + 273 = 773\ \mathrm{K}\), \(k = 1.6 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{M^{-1}s^{-1}}\), \(E_a = 56\ \mathrm{kJ/mol} = 56 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J/mol}\), frequency factor \(\mathrm{A} = ?\)

The Arrhenius equation \(k = \mathrm{A}\,e^{-E_a/RT}\) in logarithmic form (Eq. 6.19 converted to base \(10\)) gives

\(\log_{10}\mathrm{A} = \log_{10}k + \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,RT}\)

\(\dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,RT} = \dfrac{56 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}}{2.303 \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}mol^{-1}} \times 773\ \mathrm{K}} = \dfrac{56 \times 10^{3}}{14802} = 3.784\)

\(\log_{10}k = \log_{10}(1.6 \times 10^{3}) = 3.204\)

Hence

\(\log_{10}\mathrm{A} = 3.204 + 3.784 = 6.988\)

\(\mathrm{A} = \text{antilog } 6.988 = 9.72 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{M^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\)

The frequency factor is \(9.72 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{M^{-1}s^{-1}}\). It carries the same units as \(k\), since the exponential factor is dimensionless.

For a first order reaction the integrated rate law, Eq. (6.7), gives the time in terms of the fraction of reactant remaining:

\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\)

**Time for \(90\%\) completion.** If \(90\%\) has reacted, \(10\%\) remains. Taking \([\mathrm{A}]_0 = 100\) gives \([\mathrm{A}]_t = 10\), so

\(t_{90} = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log_{10}\dfrac{100}{10} = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log_{10} 10 = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \times 1 = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\)

**Time for \(99.9\%\) completion.** If \(99.9\%\) has reacted, \(0.1\%\) remains, so \([\mathrm{A}]_t = 0.1\) and

\(t_{99.9} = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log_{10}\dfrac{100}{0.1} = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log_{10} 1000 = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \times 3 = \dfrac{3 \times 2.303}{k}\)

**Ratio.** Dividing one by the other, the factor \(2.303/k\) cancels:

\(\dfrac{t_{99.9}}{t_{90}} = \dfrac{3 \times 2.303/k}{2.303/k} = 3\)

Hence \(t_{99.9} = 3\,t_{90}\): the time required for \(99.9\%\) completion is three times the time required for \(90\%\) completion, whatever the value of \(k\).

Given : \(t = 40\) min for \(30\%\) decomposition, \(t_{1/2} = ?\)

If \(30\%\) has decomposed then \(70\%\) remains, so taking \([\mathrm{A}]_0 = 100\) gives \([\mathrm{A}]_t = 70\).

For a first order reaction,

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t} = \dfrac{2.303}{40\ \mathrm{min}}\log_{10}\dfrac{100}{70}\)

\(= \dfrac{2.303 \times 0.1549}{40} = 8.918 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

Hence

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k} = \dfrac{0.693}{8.918 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}} = 77.7\ \mathrm{min}\)

The half life of the reaction is about \(77.7\) minutes.

[Textbook misprint: the relation is printed as \(\log_{10} k = 14.34 - 1.25 \times 10^{4}\ T\), with the division sign dropped. As printed, \(\log_{10}k\) would be linear in \(T\) itself rather than in \(1/T\), which is not the Arrhenius form and yields no activation energy at all; the coefficient would also carry the wrong dimensions. The intended relation is \(\log_{10} k = 14.34 - \dfrac{1.25 \times 10^{4}}{T}\), and the book's own printed answer of \(239.3\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}\) is what that reading gives. The solution below uses it.]

Eq. (6.20) gives the Arrhenius equation in the straight line form

\(\log_{10}k = -\dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\cdot\dfrac{1}{T} + \log_{10}\mathrm{A}\)

Comparing this with the given relation

\(\log_{10}k = 14.34 - \dfrac{1.25 \times 10^{4}}{T}\)

term by term, the coefficient of \(1/T\) must match:

\(\dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R} = 1.25 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{K}\)

Hence

\(E_a = 2.303 \times R \times 1.25 \times 10^{4}\)

\(= 2.303 \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}mol^{-1}} \times 1.25 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{K}\)

\(= 19.15 \times 1.25 \times 10^{4} = 2.393 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(= 239.3\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

The activation energy of the reaction is \(239.3\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}\). (The intercept \(14.34\) gives \(\log_{10}\mathrm{A}\), so \(\mathrm{A} = 2.19 \times 10^{14}\), but the question asks only for \(E_a\).)

Given : \(T = 300\ \mathrm{K}\), \(E_a = 50\ \mathrm{kJ/mol} = 50 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J/mol}\), \(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\)

Section 6.6.4 gives the fraction of molecules possessing energy greater than \(E_a\) as

\(f = e^{-E_a/RT}\)

First evaluate the exponent:

\(\dfrac{E_a}{RT} = \dfrac{50 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}}{8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}mol^{-1}} \times 300\ \mathrm{K}} = \dfrac{50 \times 10^{3}}{2494.2} = 20.05\)

Taking base ten logarithms,

\(\log_{10} f = -\dfrac{20.05}{2.303} = -8.705\)

\(f = \text{antilog}(-8.705) = 1.97 \times 10^{-9} \approx 2 \times 10^{-9}\)

The fraction is about \(2 \times 10^{-9}\), that is only about two molecules in every thousand million collide with an energy equal to or greater than the activation energy. This is why, as the chapter's "Do you know?" box notes, only a very small proportion of collisions is sufficiently energetic to lead to reaction.
